Pele Yoetz 120:3: And just as the virtue of one who studies novel Torah insights is great, correspondingly it is bad for whoever loves to hear novelties and vanities of this world - his evil is great, for through this he increases the neglect of Torah, breaking out at every command, and these things confuse his mind at the time of prayer, and his entire service is invalid. And let the man whose inclination has overpowered him, and who has grown accustomed to loving to hear novelties, muster his strength to hasten his own escape and press himself to hate the novelties that are not needed for his livelihood, saying: what benefit and what does knowledge of the world's vanities add for me? Absence is better than the presence of this evil. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Ketubot 5b): a person should not let his ears hear idle words, for they are the first to be scorched among the limbs. And for every good thing one is not accustomed to, and to withdraw one's hand from doing every evil one is accustomed to, strengthening is needed, and one must wage war against the evil inclination with stratagems - and this is one of them: let him strengthen himself to act with valor and turn evil into good, and the LORD shall grant the good.
Pele Yoetz 121:1: Weak - Let the weak say, "I am mighty," and at a time of weakness this is recognized - one who loves the LORD with all his heart shall not abandon the service of the LORD, its master, at all, but shall press himself to do the will of his Maker. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Shabbat 83b), on the verse "when a man dies in a tent," that even at the time of death one should occupy himself with Torah, and "according to the pain is the reward." However, an obligation rests upon whoever is weak to strive to make himself healthy with remedies, and he shall eat and drink even more than he has, and it shall be counted a mitzvah for him, and the LORD shall repay him. Go out and learn from what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 129a), that whoever is lenient regarding the meal after bloodletting, they are lenient with him regarding his sustenance from Heaven, and they say, "he did not have mercy on his own life, shall we have mercy on him?" And there is a time for every desire (Ecclesiastes 3:1) - a time to fast and afflict oneself, and a time to strive to make one's body healthy. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, have already warned us that a person should always be careful about the morning meal, and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said many virtues about the morning meal (Bava Metzia 107b), in a manner that on a day when he eats, he shall eat immediately after the morning prayer, and shall not fail to taste something in the morning before his senses grow weak. And likewise, at every hour that he is hungry, he shall eat, and shall eat meat and drink wine and all things that strengthen a person's body for the sake of Heaven, so that he can serve his Creator as is proper to do. However, he should not let his inclination lead him to say that he is weak and cannot serve his Creator, and that he needs abundant eating and drinking in order to be healthy and strong for the service of the blessed Name, for shall not God search this out, for He knows the truth of matters? And these are things that have a measure - one should not add and should not subtract - and through this he shall find rest for his body and his soul.
Pele Yoetz 122:1: Dream - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 55a), on the verse (Ecclesiastes 3:14), "and God has made it so that men should fear before Him" - this refers to a bad dream. And they also said (Shabbat 11a): a fast is as beneficial for a dream as fire for tow. And they said (Berachot 31b) that whoever fasts a dream-fast on the very day, even on the Sabbath, they tear up his decree of seventy years. And they said (Gittin 52a): the words of dreams neither raise up nor bring down. And they said (Berachot 55b): a dream not interpreted is like a letter not read. And they said (ibid.) that they show a good man a bad dream, and its sadness is its own interpretation - and the meaning of the matter is that it is better not to be concerned about dreams at all and not to be frightened at all, so as not to worsen one's fortune, and one should not tell his dream to anyone, for even to the greatest of the great, "dreams speak falsely," and especially in such an orphaned generation, there is no such man found whose soul ascends to the academy on high and to whom the future is revealed, as was the practice among the ancient holy ones, our early Rabbis - and by chance there may be someone who merits having the future revealed to him through an angel, but generally the power of imagination operates without the intellect, thinking thoughts of west and east, north and south. And some dreams arise from one's own thoughts on his bed, and some are confused dreams according to what bile predominates due to excessive eating and drinking or due to sadness and the like, and some are cases where spirits, demons, and night-spirits mock the soul while it is in the air of the world and show it false words like the barking of dogs, and sometimes they also inform it of some true word of what is destined to happen - in a manner that it is better not to be concerned at all.
Pele Yoetz 122:2: And especially on the Sabbath, the halachic authorities have already written (Magen Avraham, siman 288:5) that they permitted fasting only for one whose soul is grieved and for whom the fast itself is a delight, but if he is not worried and does not wish to fast, he has lost nothing - but to exempt him with nothing at all is impossible, and one must be concerned lest Heaven wished to have mercy on him and inform him, so that he take it to heart and redeem his own soul, and if he is not concerned at all, it turns out that he is liable for his own soul. Therefore, this is my way: when a person tells me he has dreamed a bad dream, I say to him, "do not fear and do not be afraid, for the words of dreams neither raise up nor bring down, and all is vanity and vexation of spirit - but there is no loss if you fast, if you can, and distribute money to charity and perform the order of Pidyon Nefesh [redemption of the soul] and the like, to take to heart to repent of the transgressions in your hand." This is the necessary, good, and beneficial matter every day and every hour. And let the one who dreamed a dream say: why should I fear? What has the master of the dream told me that is new - that I am destined to die? This I already know, and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, have informed us in saying (Avot 2:10), "repent one day before your death" - let him repent today lest he die tomorrow. And this is clear truth, but dreams are vain, a work of delusion.
Pele Yoetz 122:3: But in any case it is fitting to be concerned with the words of the master of the dream if he is about to go on a journey or by sea, and the master of the dream told him not to go - he must be concerned with these words and refrain from going. And likewise it is not good to tell others if he has dreamed about them a dream that seems to him not good, especially if the dreamer is a poor man, for they shall immediately say, "behold, the master of dreams interprets it for his own benefit." And it is best not to dig and strive to know the interpretations of dreams, for "he who adds knowledge adds sorrow" (Ecclesiastes 1:18), and "he who walks in innocence walks securely," and happy is the man who is always fearful even without a dream, and let him consider that man is given as grass, and he is destined for all the evils that stir to come into the world, and let him do whatever is in his power to do - repentance and good deeds, which are like a shield against calamity (Avot 4:11; Pirkei D'Rabbi Eliezer 43). And if he dreamed on the Sabbath or on other days when it is forbidden to fast, it is best that he not worry and not fast, but rather accept upon himself to fast two weekdays, and say the supplication our Rabbis instituted to say at the time the priests spread their hands, and also perform the "improvement of the dream" as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, taught us (Berachot 55b), and let his heart be settled and secure in the LORD without fear or apprehension, and the LORD shall be a shield and buckler to him.
Pele Yoetz 123:1: Covetousness - Well known is the great evil of covetousness. And the commentators have written that it is the tenth of the Ten Commandments and is the greatest of them all, for through covetousness one can come to transgress the entire Torah. And whoever strives to take his fellow's possession, whether for free or for money, transgresses "you shall not covet." And even if he did not strive but only thought in his heart that he wished this item to come to him, he has transgressed the negative commandment of "you shall not desire" (Deuteronomy 5:18). And one must strengthen himself and consider that everything is vanity of vanities, things without substance, and he shall not covet and shall not desire and shall not ask for an item as a gift from his fellow, for he immediately transgresses "you shall not covet," and if the giver does not give with a generous eye, there is also an element of robbery. Of such a case it is said (Proverbs 15:27), "he who hates gifts shall live." And likewise he should not strive to have an item sold to him unless he knows that its owner is planning to sell it. And if he wishes to desire, let him desire thus: would that the blessed Name provide me with such an item! This too is vanity and vexation of spirit - rather, let a man covet to attain wisdom and understanding and good traits and uprightness, and to resemble the ancient holy ones. Such a case is a mitzvah, to be jealous, to covet, and to love - this he shall answer his inclination when it wishes to entice him and lead him on a bad path: let him exchange it and turn evil into good (Leviticus 27:10), and through this he shall be saved from destruction, and the blessing of good shall come upon him.
Pele Yoetz 124:1: Support - Support given by the hand of those who support students of Torah is a precious stone; it gives life to its possessors, it is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it (Proverbs 3:18), and its deeds shall praise it in the gates (Proverbs 31:31). And well known is their saying, of blessed memory (Kohelet Rabbah 23[?]), that the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to make shade and a canopy for those who perform mitzvot beside those who possess Torah, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 7:12), "in the shadow of wisdom, in the shadow of money." And they further said (Bamidbar Rabbah 13:17) that Zebulun, who supported, was mentioned before Issachar, who studied, for greater is one who causes others to act than one who acts himself. And they said that he who shares [supports Torah study] shares equally in the World to Come with the master of Torah. Who has seen such a thing and who has heard the like, and would not therefore do this - to give a little money, a thing without substance, vanity of vanities, to purchase delicacies for his own soul and a good portion in the World to Come, like the Torah scholars who have no rest in this world and do not give sleep to their eyes nor slumber to their eyelids, and live a life of pain for the sake of the Torah - while the good-hearted rich man always drinks, and is considered as though he sits and studies like the Torah scholar, and shall receive a portion equal to his? Whoever the LORD has graced with wealth and does not do this shall be called a fool and a simpleton, for this is comparable to one who finds an opportunity to buy a pearl and a precious stone for a mere penny and does not wish to buy it - there is no greater fool and boor than this. And what shall the wealthy of the people answer on the day of reckoning, who have no leisure to touch a book and spend so many, many expenditures on trivial things, and even for transgression, and give no thought to doing this and supporting students of Torah - shame and disgrace shall cover them.
Pele Yoetz 124:2: However, in order to be like Issachar and Zebulun, one must provide the Torah scholar with enough for his need, so that he shall have no worry at all - and it is better to support one Torah scholar and give him enough for his need than to maintain a study hall of ten Torah scholars and give them each a small stipend - this is not the way to share equally.
Pele Yoetz 124:3: And even though he supports students of Torah, this does not exempt him from engaging in Torah according to his ability in times of leisure - for only the Torah scholar whose Torah is his profession, who has studied the entire Torah, is not given permission to engage in idle matters, except at a time that is neither day nor night, as it is written (Joshua 1:8), "and you shall meditate on it day and night," as brought in the Talmud (Menachot 99b). Rather, this is the whole fruit of the supporter: that it is counted for him, at the time he is engaged in business, as though he were engaged in Torah.
Pele Yoetz 124:4: And behold, the Torah scholar who has even a small amount of his own, it is fitting for him to be frugal and content, and not agree to take a stipend and sell a portion of his Torah, for all desirable things cannot compare to it. And see in the Holy Zohar (chapter, page 88b) the story of Rabbi Yosei ben Pazzi, who returned the gold to the rich man, saying that words of Torah are more precious than gold and fine gold - see there. And certainly, if half of his portion in the World to Come is diminished and given to the rich man, it turns out that the Torah scholar makes a bad exchange, for "better one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come than all the life of this world" (Avot 4:17). And if we say that nothing is diminished, and it is like lighting one candle from another, the matter is difficult, for if so, one who studies Torah out of poverty would be equal to one who studies out of prosperity, and the heart hesitates. And this is especially so given what the Holy Zohar reveals (ibid.), and also what the halachic authorities have written (Pitchei Teshuvah, Yoreh De'ah, siman 246, note 2), that one who studies for a stipend does not fulfill the mitzvah of "and you shall meditate" - see there. In a manner that, as it appears, if the Torah scholar finds someone who wishes to give him as a gift and as charity, he may accept it - but on condition of sharing equally like Issachar and Zebulun, or on condition that his teacher's Torah be sold to him, he should not wish nor accept, for this is like giving gold and pearls for lead and dust.
Pele Yoetz 124:5: But however, if he cannot support himself in any other way, and "if there is no flour, there is no Torah," and its end is nullification, dragging sin along with it (Avot 3:17), it is fitting for him to accept - not only when he gives half his portion for the World to Come, but even if he must give his entire portion, let the faithful servant say: I have loved my master, and better for me one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world, in settlement, that I be able to serve a complete service as is proper to do, than all the life of the World to Come - and how important in my eyes is the entire World to Come compared to whatever I can do to give more peace of mind to my Former? And those who seek the LORD shall not lack any good (Psalms 34:11).
Pele Yoetz 124:6: And it is known that in all matters the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, applies: "your own life takes precedence" (Bava Metzia 62a), and "your own poor take precedence" (ibid. 71a) - all the more so in this matter, that it takes precedence to study, and if he cannot study, let him hold fast in his stronghold for his sons, that Torah be their profession. And likewise, the brothers upon whom has fallen the lot of a Torah scholar brother shall support him, and likewise all who are of their family and their father's house take precedence over strangers, and this is a merit for them and for their father's soul. And thus, if one alone cannot support him, let them all bear the burden together of their Torah scholar brother, in a manner that his Torah be his profession and he not need to interrupt his studies and have no worry, but rather his mind shall be clear and settled upon him - and besides that they shall receive good reward for their labor, they shall carry a blessing from their father and mother, and there is no honoring of father and mother greater than this. And I have already written about this above under the entry "Love of Students of Torah" - see there. And whoever does not have the strength to support students of Torah with his own money shall support them with his own body, standing to serve them and buy their needs, or if he can do business for a Torah scholar - great is such service, and like the portion of one who goes down to war is the portion of one who stays by the baggage (I Samuel 30:24) - every person is obligated only according to his own measure; whatever is in his power to do, let him do, to give peace of mind to his Former and to bring merit to his own nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, for this is his portion.
Pele Yoetz 124:7: And it is included in the mitzvah of support to strengthen the hands of students of Torah and those who perform mitzvot by honoring and exalting them, and not to be a cause of locking the door before students of Torah and those who perform mitzvot by disgracing them and mocking them, God forbid. And behold, the great ones who have knowledge and understanding and have already entered into the category of masters of Torah and masters of good deeds - there is not so much concern that they shall turn back because of the mockery of the complacent. However, if strengthening is needed, it is for the young, or those beginning to be educated in Torah and mitzvot - for them, all the more so, is zeal needed to strengthen their hands with good things, with gifts and presents according to the child's own understanding and his own will, so that from doing it not for its own sake, he shall come to do it for its own sake. And those who see the honor of the Torah and of those who study it, and the honor accorded to those who perform mitzvot, their hearts shall be kindled to draw near to the craft, and their hearts shall be kindled, saying: if in this world it is thus for those who do His will, all the more so in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 125:1: Education - It is written (Proverbs 22:6), "train up a child according to his way, even when he is old he shall not depart from it." This is a mitzvah of the father toward the son: to educate him in Torah and in mitzvot, for this is the entire fruit of sons - to raise them upon Torah and upon service - for if, God forbid, they become corrupt sons, absence is better than the presence of this evil. And just as one must educate them in Torah and mitzvot, so too must one teach and educate them in proper conduct and good traits and uprightness, in a manner that all who see them recognize that they are offspring the LORD has blessed. And let him educate them and accustom them to the trait of contentment, so that they not be obsessed with pursuing fine food and fine clothing. And even if the LORD has graced him with wealth, let him accustom his sons to be content with a little good, so that they not be distressed in times of trouble. And whoever wishes to educate his sons and accustom them to the way of the good shall not show them a pleasant face, but shall always strike them and rebuke them with his mouth, in a manner that they not become proud and that they not have longing [for indulgence]. And even if he has only one son, he shall always show him open rebuke rather than hidden love, until he grows up. For "he who spares his rod hates his son," but "he who loves him disciplines him diligently" (Proverbs 13:24). And go out and learn what happened to King David, peace be upon him, with Absalom, for his father never grieved him by saying, "why have you done so?" (II Samuel 15-17), and "the hands of compassionate women have cooked their own children" (Lamentations 4:10), for "folly is bound up in the heart of a child; the rod of discipline shall drive it far from him" (Proverbs 22:15). And everything follows the child's own understanding and his own years - he shall vary his approach with him: sometimes with strikes, sometimes with rebukes, sometimes with requests, sometimes with blessings, sometimes with gifts and presents, sometimes with good words. And let him educate them in the honor of creatures, that they not be brazen-faced and stiff-necked, and that they be among those who are insulted rather than those who insult. And let him keep them far from the company of bad friends, and from oaths, and from jest, and from ugliness, and from the like. And wisdom and knowledge are needed to descend into the inner chambers of the sons' hearts and vary the approach with them as is proper according to their own understanding and their own years. And above all, let him pour out his soul before the LORD, that his own sins not withhold the good from him, and that all his offspring be a holy seed of holies, offspring of [worthy] men.
Pele Yoetz 125:2: And regarding daughters too, an obligation rests to educate them and accustom them in every craft and every perfection and every good trait, and especially that they be content with little, and that their eyes be generous, and that they not be lazy nor talkative, and that she rise while it is still night and perform all her deeds with alacrity, cleanliness, propriety, and privacy, and every order of worthy women, in a manner that her deeds shall praise her in the gates, and she shall find favor and good sense. And extra caution is especially needed regarding daughters, for one does not know the portion of their lot, and if, God forbid, she finds a harsh husband and a harsh mother-in-law and harsh members of the household, and she has been taught grandiose ways and inferior traits, woe to her and to her bad fortune. And also, "a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised" (Proverbs 31:30). And an obligation rests upon her father and mother to educate her and accustom her in the blessings over benefits and in prayers and the mitzvot of niddah, challah, and salting [of meat], that she be expert in them in all their fine details, and all the laws and mitzvot of women that she shall teach her, and that she be learned in every single trait, and that she be modest - "all glorious is the king's daughter within" (Psalms 45:14). These are some aspects of the ways of education - let the wise man hear and add learning, and through this he shall rejoice in his own offspring in this world and his soul shall exult in the World to Come. And I have already written about this above under the entry "Love of One's Offspring" - see there, and in my other holy writings, and I return to repeat these matters from time to time, for it is fitting to repeat words of ethics and fear of the LORD and good conduct, for a person's inclination renews itself and is aroused momentarily to test him. Therefore, "let my teaching drip like rain, let my speech distill as the dew" - perhaps I shall be able to strike it and drive it out, with the help of Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 126:1: Assembly - Well known is the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Rashi, Bechukotai 26:8, in the name of Torat Kohanim): few performing a mitzvah are not comparable to many performing a mitzvah, for it is greatly elevated the more there are gathered together. And "in a multitude of people is the king's glory" (Proverbs 14:28). And behold, regarding prayers, it is a great necessity to pray with the congregation, for the prayer of an individual, especially in such an orphaned generation, is almost called rejected, for many conditions are needed for it to be with great intention, since prayer without intention is like a body without a soul (Abravanel, Avot 2:13; Midrash Shmuel 2:15). And the person must be cleansed of sin so that his prayer ascend above, favorably before the LORD - such a thing, perhaps. And who is it whose heart is so full and who trusts in these generations to pray alone and that his prayer shall ascend favorably? This is our comfort in this matter: for the mighty God shall not reject, and even though "they beguile Him with their mouth and lie to Him with their tongue, and their heart is not steadfast with Him," He, being merciful, shall atone. Therefore the man who desires life shall not pray alone except in complete compulsion, for he shall lose much good - the response of craftsmen [the congregation's Amen], "yehei shemei rabba," "barchu," and "kedushah" - and his own prayer is turbid and barren, bearing no fruit.
Pele Yoetz 126:2: However, regarding Torah study too, Torah studied by the many is preferable, and in my opinion it is better to teach Psalms with the many than to teach the laws of skin afflictions and tent-defilement alone. And behold, King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 119:63), "I am a companion to all who fear You." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Chagigah 9b): "and what is lacking cannot be counted" (Ecclesiastes 1:15) - this refers to one whose friends were counted for a matter of mitzvah and he was not counted with them. Behold, therefore, it is good for a man to join every group performing a mitzvah that exists in the city, that his portion be with them, for a person does not know the reward given for mitzvot, and when he shall see the reward given to the righteous in the future to come, and he was not counted among them, his teeth shall grind and melt and he shall not be able to repair it. Therefore, while he is still alive, let him do whatever is in his power to do, and let his hand be in everything. However, one must be careful with these fellowships that make agreements and accept upon themselves conditions with complete obligation and oaths, and by the force of oaths and agreements sign themselves to keep and fulfill - one should not sign himself and should not enter unless on condition of doing what he has accepted, for if he does not fulfill it, he has a transgression in his hand, and it turns out that his reward comes out at his own loss. And this stumbling block lies under the hand of many holy fellowships, and it is fitting to open one's eyes and warn the people and inform them of the severity of transgressing oaths, agreements, and undertakings. And the wise man has his eyes in his head, and shall sign to an agreement only matters that can easily be maintained without transgressing. And they shall also leave room to reconsider according to the time and according to the people, in a manner that no mishap come forth and their fellowship be pleasing to them and a great deliverance.
Pele Yoetz 127:1: Companionship - How good is companionship, to the point that they said (Mivchar HaPeninim 20:11; Yerushalmi Horayot 3:5; Meiri, Proverbs 17:17): a person without a companion is like the left hand without the right - only let the companion be a good one, God-fearing and turning away from evil. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Yevamot 63a): descend a step, choose a groomsman [i.e., companion]. And it is good for a man to have a good friend, a beloved companion, to whom he reveals all his secrets and with whom he consults on everything he wishes to do. And even if he is a great sage, let him take counsel from the small, for "a wise man listens to counsel" (Proverbs 12:15), for "two are better than one" (Ecclesiastes 4:9). And who is greater than the Holy One, blessed be He, who said (Genesis 1:26), "let us make man" - and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 38b) that He consulted the ministering angels, to teach a person knowledge, that even the great shall take counsel from the small, for many times his own eye deceives him, and "according to the difficulty is the error" (Bava Metzia 96b), and every man is a liar. And when he takes counsel, if it does not help, he loses nothing, and if it does not seem right in his eyes, let him do what is right in his own eyes. And we learned (Proverbs 3:5), "and do not lean on your own understanding," and "salvation is in a multitude of counselors." And all the more so, to engage in words of Torah, companionship is needed, for they sharpen each other in halachah. And well known is the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Ta'anit 7a), on the verse (Jeremiah 50:36), "a sword upon the boasters, and they shall become fools" - may the Merciful One save us - this refers to Torah scholars who sit alone and study. But one must choose good friends who are agreeable to each other in halachah and acknowledge the truth - not so when they are not good, who gore each other with quarrelsome words, and great is the accusation, hatred, and rivalry - such a case is absence of good. And if a good friend cannot be found, let his students be his friends, for a certain sage already said, "much have I learned from my teachers, and from my friends more, and from my students more than all of them" (Ta'anit 7a).
Pele Yoetz 127:2: And behold, regarding judgment and rendering decisions, one must be among those who fear to render decisions and should not judge alone, so as not to err, and so that a share of responsibility reach them, as they said "let a portion reach them from the wooden beam" (Sanhedrin 7b). And if he is in a place where there are no [other qualified] men, let him be his own companion - that is, let him dig several tunnels and take sides to refute his own opinion and reasoning, and strive with all his strength to find fault with his own view and to reconsider his obligation, and through this his righteousness shall emerge clear as the dawn, and he shall render a true judgment in its truth. And likewise in his engagement with Torah, when some difficulty or resolution comes to him that seems very good in his eyes, let him strive greatly to reject it and refute it, and through the debate he multiplies with himself, the truth shall be clarified. And companionship is most beneficial for those who fear the LORD and esteem His Name, "then those who feared the LORD spoke, one to another." So is our obligation and so is fitting for us. "Take counsel together, what is the straight path," and "let each man help his fellow, and say to his brother, be strong" (Isaiah 41:6), and let us strengthen ourselves for the sake of our God. However, there is no love and companionship except among equals, similar in traits and knowledge - then "brothers dwell together" and shall not be separated. But this is a difficult thing to find - if he finds it, let him hold fast to it and not let it go.
Pele Yoetz 127:3: And just as a good friend brings redemption, correspondingly a bad friend causes great evil, for it is impossible that one not learn from him and not do as he does, unless willingly, for the sake of honor or shame. And if he is saved from bad speech, he is not saved from hearing evil; and if he is saved from doing evil, he is not saved from transgressing the mitzvah of rebuke, and the young man shall bear grief and sighing on his account. Therefore every person shall be careful and stand guard over his sons to separate them from bad companions and seat them among the knees of Torah scholars, for "a man of friends is to be broken" [i.e., must choose them carefully] (Proverbs 18:24), and "he who walks with the wise shall become wise" (ibid. 13:20). And in any case, if he has no good friend, let him take counsel with his own wife, as we find (Berachot 27b) regarding Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah when they wished to appoint him Nasi. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Bava Metzia 59a): if your wife is short, bend down and whisper to her. And it is written (Malachi 2:14), "yet she is your companion and your wife by covenant."
Pele Yoetz 128:1: Life - Whoever wishes to live shall put himself to death - so said our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Tamid 32a). And there are two aspects to this. The first is that he not conduct himself as one who is pampered and trained in pleasures, eating to satiety and covering himself lavishly - for if at some time he finds himself in siege and distress and cannot conduct himself as he has been trained, his life is not truly life, and he is destined to go out to bad conduct and to steal and to rob, and whatever comes to his hand to do evil, he does, and he conducts business dishonestly, for habit becomes to him an obligation, and "for a piece of bread a man transgresses" (Proverbs 28:21). Not so one who puts himself to death and trains himself not to be exacting about anything, treating everything equally whether lacking or abundant - he shall live in ease, a good and long life, and shall not need to be a man of deceit.
Pele Yoetz 128:2: Behold, therefore, it is good for a man, even if the LORD has graced him with wealth, honor, and abundant possessions and food, not to accustom his sons to grandiose things and human pleasures, for he does not know what a day may bring. And the Torah testified that once a child is trained in excessive eating and drinking, even when he grows old he shall not depart from it, and in the end he shall rob people (Sanhedrin 72a[?]). And therefore the Torah said (Deuteronomy 21:18), "if a man has a stubborn and rebellious son" - let him die innocent and let him not die guilty (Sanhedrin 71b[?]). And we have already seen with our own eyes and heard with our own ears how many, through being accustomed to grandiose things and pleasures, ended up going out to bad conduct, and their end was bad, may the Merciful One save us. And even if he does not go out to bad conduct, in any case he shall live a life of pain, and many times he shall hunger and not eat, for man does not live by bread alone. But one who conducts himself to be content with whatever comes to his hand shall be satisfied with bread, and it is good for him in this. And there is another interpretation: that whoever wishes to live the true life, the life of the World to Come, shall put himself to death in this world for the sake of Torah and service, in the manner they explained (Berachot 63b[?]), "when a man dies in a tent" (Numbers 19:14). And it is written (Psalms 44:23), "for Your sake we are killed all day long."
Pele Yoetz 128:3: And behold, from one side it would be fitting for a person to despise the life of this world, which is a world of grief and sighing, and even its good things are not good, for they are vanity. However, from another side, it is fitting to desire life and love days in this world more than the life of the World to Come, for they said (Avot 4:17): better one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world than all the life of the World to Come. For it is good for us to serve our Creator and give peace of mind before His throne of glory even for one hour, more than all the life of the World to Come, and this can be attained only in the life of this world, for the days of the World to Come are days in which there is no desire, neither merit nor obligation.
Pele Yoetz 128:4: For this let every pious man pray, and for this shall he direct himself when he desires and seeks life - not in order to attain the joy of seeing his children, and to see grandchildren, and the like, for all this is vanity, and were it only for this, it would be better to be in the world of truth, and "better one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come than all the life of this world," and the commentators have already explained the verse (Psalms 34:13), "who is the man who desires life, who loves days to see good?" - meaning to say, who is this lowly and despised one who desires life in order to see good, in the manner of "who is this uncircumcised Philistine?" (I Samuel 17:26) - rather, what he desires in life shall be specifically to serve his Creator and to give peace of mind before His throne of glory. And whoever goes deep into this shall strive greatly to spend all his life in the service of the blessed Name, and "in all his ways he shall know Him," and all his deeds shall be for the sake of Heaven, and he shall have great regard for the time he is alive, not to spend it in vain, for it is more precious than all the life of the World to Come. And for this reason too, an obligation rests upon every man to guard his health and be very careful for his own soul, so as not to lose much good that he can acquire in one hour of the life of this world. And whoever does not guard himself against everything evil is liable for his own soul, and is destined to give judgment and account for all the loss of time he causes.
Pele Yoetz 128:5: And the sages of ethics have already written this understanding: that if they were to say to a person, "for how much will you sell one year of your life," or even one day, or even one hour, if they gave him all the silver and gold in the world he would utterly scorn them - and how does he give away his own life for free and spend it in vanity, consuming his days in smoke, or in jest and frivolity, or in forbidden things, sins and transgressions, in a manner that his death is far better than his life? Is there any greater folly than this? Whoever desires life shall have regard for every moment of his life, not to spend it in vain, more than he would have regard for much silver and gold, and shall always, without interruption, be occupied with the service of his Creator, whether in deed, in speech, or in thought.
Pele Yoetz 128:6: And the service of thought - to fear and love the honored and awesome LORD and to cleave to Him and the like - is a constant service, and he can perform it always, whether sitting or walking, whether lying down or rising. And while he is occupied with his business and busy with his labors, and while he is occupied with eating and drinking, or standing in the synagogue, let this service not be lacking to the good and upright man. And those who make their paths straight always have the LORD before them, and this is the whole of man.
Pele Yoetz 128:7: And whoever does not have the strength to unify his own heart to think pure thoughts always shall choose the easier path - "the voice is the voice of Jacob" - and not let his mouth cease from study on the Sabbath and while walking in a clean place, and let him study what he is expert in and fluent with by heart, such as the passage of the daily offering, the Shema passage, and the like, and likewise some fluent Mishnayot, such as "Yehudah ben Tema," "Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya," and the like - repeating it even a thousand thousand times. And so said our Rabbis (Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Zuta 2), that even if a person studies all day only the verse "and Lotan's sister was Timna" (Genesis 36:22), the Holy One, blessed be He, establishes for him a reward as though he were occupied with the laws of skin afflictions and tent-defilement. And every person is obligated only according to his own ability - such is his obligation, and nothing exempts him from it. And although there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin in this matter, in any case let him do whatever is in his power to do, and remember his Holy Rock, and choose the lesser evil, and not turn to his own understanding - and whoever comes to purify himself is assisted.
Pele Yoetz 129:1: Strength - Strength is necessary for everything a person is charged to do, and for everything he is warned not to do, whether optional matters or obligatory matters - for if, when it becomes somewhat difficult for him, he withdraws his hand, he shall lose much good, and shall go from evil to evil, for there is nothing good that does not require effort and toil. Regarding optional matters it is written (Genesis 3:19), "by the sweat of your brow you shall eat bread." And regarding matters of mitzvah, a person's own inclination overpowers him and stands at his right hand to be his adversary, and "man is born to toil." And one must strengthen himself with a mighty hand to fulfill every matter. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Berachot 32b): three things require strengthening: Torah, good deeds, and proper conduct - that is, livelihood - and especially in matters of mitzvah, for the inclination of a person's heart is evil, and it is fire, like a man of war it stirs up jealousy. And if a person does not strengthen himself with great vigor and might, "we would perish, we would be lost," God forbid, for little by little he shall go on diminishing, for today his inclination says to him, "do such and such," and so on, until it says to him, "go worship idols," or something resembling idol worship (Shabbat 105b), until it becomes to him as fully permitted, and there is neither seeker nor searcher. And even if his ears hear what the mitzvah is, or he hears that there is a prohibition in the matter, "the wicked shall not forsake his way," and the world conducts itself as is its custom - this is the evil of man on earth because of our many sins, and therefore "the harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved" (Jeremiah 8:20).
Pele Yoetz 129:2: But this is the teaching of the man who is a Jew and whose soul desires to be a servant of God: regarding everything he knows to be a transgression, or that this is the straight path, he shall wage war with stratagems against his inclination, and shall strengthen and fortify himself with great vigor and might, with all firmness, to stand guard, to keep and to do and to fulfill every matter even unto death, and not transgress, for death is chosen over life so as not to transgress the mitzvah of our King, our God, the King of the universe. And just as his inclination renews itself against him and grows stronger every day, so must he grow stronger against it and strengthen himself every day. And whatever a man wishes to do, he can do - even the most difficult thing shall not be difficult for him when he wishes, and he has no room for exemption on the day of judgment. And if his beginning is of pain, his end shall increase, for all beginnings are difficult, and afterward, once he has practiced for some time, his heart shall be steady and faithful. And if it is exceedingly difficult for him to fulfill any mitzvah and to withdraw his hand from transgression, "according to the pain is the reward" (Avot end of ch. 5), and this is a great principle in the Torah.
Pele Yoetz 130:1: Wisdom - "Happy is the man who has found wisdom" (Proverbs 3:13) - happy is he in this world and it is good for him in the World to Come. And this is a mitzvah of the father toward the son, to raise them upon the Torah - he shall rejoice in them in this world and his soul shall delight in fatness in the World to Come. And this is a well-known and famous matter, but no person sets his heart to give his soul over to this matter and to enter into the thickness of the beam as is necessary to do, according to the abundance of the good - and all the more so does an obligation rest upon the watchmen of every city, everywhere, to stand guard over this with all their strength and with all their might, and to be careful with the children of the poor, from whom Torah shall come forth, and through this their wealth shall be great in this world and in the World to Come, for great is the one who causes to act, and it is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it. And behold, the matter of wisdom is that one know how to engage in give-and-take and dwell in the depth of halachah. And there are corrupt opinions who do not wish to tire themselves, saying: is not the essence of engaging in Torah in order to keep and to do and to fulfill? If so, it is enough for us to study summaries and legal rulings. And they are not correct in this, for it is known that the Holy One, blessed be He, rejoices in dialectical give-and-take, and whoever engages in dialectics in halachah breaks the power of the husk and separates chaff from wheat and adorns the bride, and there is no end to his reward. Behold, therefore, whoever the LORD has graced with understanding, it is fitting for him to press himself and enter into what is beyond him, and by the sweat of his brow strive and strengthen himself to enter the gates of wisdom, day by day adding knowledge, until he knows how to understand one thing from another and to render judgment on one matter from another, until he is fit to render halachic decisions in Israel. And it is known that whoever wishes to merit the crown of Torah must have extra affection and great diligence day and night, seeking to reach great heights and to understand the difficult matter with much labor and great effort. And they have already said (Megillah 6b): if someone tells you, "I have labored and not found," do not believe him. And they have already told of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, that he would toil in halachah until he sweated, and when he did not understand the depth of the halachah he would confess and weep and shed tears the number of the hairs of his head, as is written in the writings - from this let the wise man hear the precious value of wisdom, and how it is fitting to conduct oneself with wisdom and hold fast to it with great vigor and might, and according to his affection and diligence shall his wisdom grow, and the wisdom of a man shall light up his face in this world and in the World to Come, and the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the LORD, and whoever's fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom endures (Avot 3:9) - this is a great principle in the Torah.
Pele Yoetz 131:1: Desecration of the Name - It is known that desecration of the Name is more severe than all the transgressions in the Torah, to the point that our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 86a) that it is not atoned for except through repentance, suffering, Yom Kippur, and the day of death. Therefore let the man tremble and be seized, and be careful and guard against anything that constitutes desecration of the Name. And the difficult thing is that desecration of the Name depends entirely on what kind of person one is and how the world regards him - if it causes people to speak disparagingly of him, it is desecration of the Name - to the point that they said (ibid.), "for example, if I walk four cubits without Torah and without tefillin due to circumstances beyond my control, and the world does not know and thinks it is due to laziness - it is desecration of the Name." Go out and learn the severity that is in these matters. Over this let all who grieve, grieve, for who is innocent? Woe to us for the day of judgment. But every person is obligated only according to his own measure, and let him do whatever is in his power to do, and guard and be careful to the extent of his ability, and strive with all vigor to guard against ugliness and its like, and that people find no room to speak against him. And especially regarding the matter of money, great care is needed that money not be considered of any worth in his eyes in a place where there is a one-in-a-thousand concern for desecration of the Name, or a concern of robbery, or any hint of prohibition - let him overcome and cast away his silver and his gold, for it is better that he die of hunger than that he be wicked before the Omnipresent for even one hour. All the more so since those who seek the LORD shall not lack any good (Psalms 34:11).
Pele Yoetz 131:2: And especially in these generations great care and extra guarding are needed, for because of our sins, the unrestrained have multiplied, whose souls thirst to speak disparagingly of Torah scholars and of those who fear the Name and esteem it, and even if all his ways were justice, like an angel of the LORD of hosts, if it should happen that he stumbles in some small matter, whether under compulsion or by error, or if they suspect him of something he has not done, or if they hear some bad report about him, they shall not dig to know the truth of the matter, how it truly happened, but shall immediately open their mouths without restraint and mock the messengers of God. And even regarding the young who begin to study, if they do childish things, they immediately carry the Torah on their own mouths and say, "look at the son who studies Gemara," or "see the man who is a Torah scholar," or "see the man they consider pious or God-fearing - such and such are his deeds" - and no one tips the scale toward merit, but they all open toward guilt. Woe to them and to their souls, for they have repaid evil, and they shall take a leading share for the sin of desecration of the Name. And how much evil they do, speaking evil speech and causing desecration of the Name, and preventing the many from entering the path of wisdom and piety, for he fears the reproach of the base.
Pele Yoetz 131:3: And the complete men have no recourse but to strive with all their strength to do the good and the upright in the eyes of God and man, and to pour out their souls before the LORD that He set them right with good counsel and guide them in paths of righteousness. And if, despite all this, people wish to speak disparagingly of him, it is possible that there is no sin in him and they shall bear their own iniquity, for who can fulfill the obligation of pleasing every person and every opinion? Even against Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, they spoke, as it is written (Numbers 21:5), "and the people spoke against God and against Moses." And even if he does what is upright in his own eyes, thinking this is the straight path, and a mishap results and people find room to speak of the matter, it is possible that the good LORD shall atone for it, for the Torah was not given to ministering angels - only let him be deliberate, deliberate, and set his heart to think thoughts and weigh in the balance the end of a matter from its beginning, and listen to counsel, and the LORD shall not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 131:4: And we have heard a remedy for whoever has become liable to death by Heaven for the sin of desecration of the Name and the like: that he intend to give over his soul to death with a whole heart every time he recites the Shema and at the recitation of the falling on the face [Tachanun], and a good thought the Holy One, blessed be He, joins to the deed (Kiddushin 40a).
Pele Yoetz 132:1: The Sick - Regarding the sick there are two warnings: a warning to others concerning him, and a warning to himself concerning himself. The warning to others concerning him is to visit him, for it is known that this is a great mitzvah, that one enjoys its fruits in this world while the principal remains for the World to Come. And it is known that the essence of the visit is to seek mercy for him (Shabbat 12b). And I, in my poverty, have already arranged a prayer for this (and I have included it in my "Beit Tefillati"). And at the very least, every person can fulfill his obligation by saying to him, when taking leave of him, "may the Omnipresent heal you with a complete healing among the sick of His people Israel." And if he is a poor man, the essence of the mitzvah of visiting is so that he see what he lacks and what he needs, and strive to support him and sustain him with remedies and with all his needs, either from his own hand or by having others do it. And happy is Israel, that in every single city, in every single province, they hold fast to this mitzvah, and they have a holy society of acts of kindness who perform kindness with the sick and with the dead, and if they are poor, they give them a free gift, enough for their need - happy is their portion (Zohar I, 130b).
Pele Yoetz 132:2: But the mitzvah of visiting the sick is neglected, and if a rich man has a headache and does not go out to the marketplace, immediately many enter to see him - but if a poor man becomes ill, no one seeks or asks to know how he fares and what to do for him, for according to the greatness of the mitzvah, the evil inclination overpowers a person in order to make him lose much good, for besides the mitzvah itself, another benefit follows: that the living shall take to heart what is man, and why he is destined for rebukes for sin, poverty, and evil illnesses. And one mitzvah draws another, for upon seeing the distress and hardship of his fellow Israelite, his own heart shall stir with compassion, may He have mercy on him, and he shall give him according to the gift of his hand, according to the blessing the LORD has given him, and it turns out that he pursues charity and kindness, and shall find life, righteousness, and honor.
Pele Yoetz 132:3: And how good and how pleasant it would be for the members of the holy society to institute that two of them, by lot, go each day to visit the sick as a fixed practice, not to be transgressed, and if one transgresses, he shall be punished with a fine - and thus they shall bring merit to the many, for otherwise the evil inclination incites doubly and does not let a person fulfill such a great mitzvah. And let the members of the holy society also open their hands to consider the poor and give him enough for his need, and strive for his healing and his health, for whoever sustains one soul of Israel is as though he had sustained an entire world (Sanhedrin 37a), and behold, their reward is with them in this world and in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 132:4: There is another mitzvah incumbent regarding the sick: to remind him of confessions and repentance and prayer with pleasant speech, and likewise regarding the mitzvot that apply constantly, such as prayer, tzitzit, tefillin, Grace after Meals and all the blessings of enjoyment, washing of hands, and the counting of the Omer, and the like, and to say with him the order of confession, and to arrange for him a short prayer according to what kind of person he is, and to remind him to arrange his affairs - who owes him and to whom he owes - this is a great kindness toward the sick, and his own soul lives thereby, and it brings him healing of the soul and healing of the body. Happy is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds fast to it (Isaiah 56:2). And this mitzvah rests upon Torah scholars, for they have the eloquence and the capacity for it. And it is fitting for Torah scholars found in every single city to hold fast to this mitzvah with both hands, for it is great, since he acquires his own soul thereby. And truly, "he who is gracious to the poor repays his own soul, a man of kindness," and the hour requires this: to bring back a crushed man, and since he is struck by God and afflicted, his heart shall be humbled and he shall repent with a whole heart, and his repentance bears fruit, and great is the deed.
Pele Yoetz 132:5: And if, God forbid, he reaches the gates of death, it is the mitzvah of others regarding him to stand by him at the time this is found, this death, with faithful recitation of verses and supplications, and especially the recitation of the forty-two-letter Name in the order "Ana BeKoach," recited backward, which is greatly effective to ease the pangs of death from him, to give rest to his soul. And it is also the mitzvah of others regarding him to strive that he be clean, and to stand over him at the time of the departure of the soul so that he not expel any of his limbs outward. These are some aspects of the ways of the mitzvah of visiting the sick - let the wise man hear and add to performing kindness, provided he manages his affairs with judgment, and it is easy for the understanding to know not to burden the sick person.
Pele Yoetz 132:6: And the warning to the sick person concerning himself: that he take to heart that a person is always destined for the day of death, and as they said (Shabbat 153a[?]), "repent one day before your death." And all the more so when he has fallen ill, they said of him (Shabbat 32a) that he is comparable to one who has been brought up to the scaffold for judgment, who needs great advocates to be saved, and they say to him, "bring merit and be acquitted," and he shall be clothed in dread. And as soon as he takes to his bed, he should not despair of calamity, and should not wait until the illness grows heavy upon him, for then perhaps he shall be unable to do anything of the ways of repentance, God forbid. Therefore, immediately and at once, let him take to heart to repent and arrange his affairs. And the hour requires him to overcome like a lion to fulfill every matter of mitzvah that comes to his hand, in order to add one more mitzvah, and let him not be lenient at the time of weighing.
